questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `++i` increments then yields 6, so `j == 6`. `i--` yields the old value 6 (`k == 6`), then `i` becomes 5.
questions.code:
#include <iostream>
int main() { int i{ 5 }; int j{ ++i }; int k{ i-- }; std::cout << j << " " << k << " " << i << "\n"; }

questions.question: Does this compile?
questions.explanation: Brace initialisation rejects *narrowing* conversions such as `double` → `int`. `int x = 3.7;` would compile (with a warning) and truncate to 3.
questions.code: int main() { int x{ 3.7 }; return x; }

questions.question: What is the type of `v` in `auto v = { 1 };`?
questions.explanation: `auto` with `= { ... }` deduces an `std::initializer_list`. That's why slide 29 says to avoid it. `auto v{ 1 };` gives an `int`.

No: defaults are only allowed in declarations
No: `rate` can't default to a double literal

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `i` is captured **by value** when the lambda is created (1), and `j` **by reference**. After `++i; ++j;` the lambda still sees `i == 1` but `j == 3`: `1 + 3 = 4`.

questions.question: Which variable must be known at compile time?
questions.explanation: `const` only means *read-only after initialisation*: the value may come from run time. `constexpr` requires a compile-time constant.

questions.question: This program receives `2147483647` (INT_MAX) on stdin. What is printing `n + 1`?
questions.explanation: Signed integer overflow is **undefined behaviour**: any outcome is allowed. UBSan reports it. (Unsigned arithmetic, by contrast, wraps around by definition.)
questions.code:
#include <iostream>
int main() { int n; std::cin >> n; std::cout << n + 1 << "\n"; }

questions.question: What does this print?
choices: It depends on the optimisation level
questions.explanation: `0.1` and `0.2` aren't exactly representable in binary floating point. `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`, which isn't `0.3`.
